content.thinking:
I'm planning a whimsical capybara model with a bird perched on its head, sketching proportions based on real capybara size—chunky barrel body, blunt head, tiny ears—then writing the generation code carefully to keep it robust against type errors.

Defining the skeleton...

For the neck I'll build a short chain from the spine tip, then add a separate head joint parented to it, aiming forward and slightly down. For the capybara's head itself I'm planning a large, boxy snout with a blunt nose and top-mounted nostrils.

Now I'm sketching the overall proportions: head roughly 0.28m long, body height around 0.55m at the shoulder with a chunky barrel-shaped torso, and short stubby legs about 0.2m tall. I'm working out a loft for the body with stations running from the hips to the shoulders, varying width and height to give it that round, whimsical capybara silhouette.

For the rigging, I'm structuring the bone hierarchy as hips, spine, and head, with the spine following the loft path and joints placed at matching points along it. I need to make sure overlapping joints at the same position along the path get deduplicated properly so the chain doesn't break, keeping things simple by favoring a single unified body structure over separate parts.

Actually safer to place hips near the rear, matching a real capybara's pelvis position, so I'll set hips at the rump and run the spine chain forward through the body. No visible tail needed, though I could add a tiny nub joint for rig completeness. Now I'm laying out the body loft stations, defining center position, width, and height at each point from rump to front to shape the rounded capybara torso.

Checking the proportions: belly clearance ends up around 0.19-0.20m which feels right for short capybara legs, and I'm adjusting the back height down slightly since 0.65m felt too tall compared to the real 0.5-0.6m range, so I'm nudging center y values lower to around 0.37-0.39.

Now I'm working out the front leg geometry — placing the shoulder root, computing the distance to the foot target, and making sure the limb length comfortably covers that span with a slight backward bend at the elbow to mimic a capybara's natural stance.

I'm naming the three joints of each limb chain (shoulder, elbow, paw) so the tip resolves correctly, then moving to the hind legs, which need three segments with deep thighs and a forward-bent knee before the hock angles back toward the foot.

I'll simplify by keeping the 3-bone hind legs since they look more anatomical, just adjusting the hip and target positions so the leg crouches naturally with the knee forward and hock back, keeping the last segment roughly vertical for a solid stance.

For the leg geometry, I'm tapering the tube radius along the chain so the thigh is thickest and it narrows toward the foot, giving a realistic chunky-but-tapered limb. For the feet, I want to add distinct toes matching capybara anatomy—four toes in front, three in back, slightly webbed with blunt nail-like tips.

I'm placing a flattened sphere as the foot pad at the leg's end, scaled unevenly so it sits low and wide, with the bottom just grazing the ground plane within the allowed sink tolerance. Small toe nubs will sit in front of the pad with darker nail caps for detail.

Now I'm turning to the head: a big, blunt, boxy shape sitting on a short thick neck in line with the body, with the head center slightly lower than the shoulder top of the back. I'm defining the skull station with its position, width, and height to start lofting the head shape from the back toward the front.

I'm continuing the loft stations down through the muzzle toward a blunt, rounded snout end, since capybaras have very tall, flat-fronted noses rather than tapered ones. I'll add a dark flattened-sphere nose pad at the tip, nostril nubs positioned high on the snout's front face, and a whimsical bump representing the morrillo gland on top of the nose for character.

Now I'm separating head construction into upper skull/muzzle loft and a distinct lower jaw piece on its own joint, since the mouth needs separate upper and lower jaw parts. The lower jaw will be narrower and set under the muzzle with a dark lip line marking the mouth seam, plus a subtle content-looking mouth curve and hints of incisor teeth for character.

For whimsy I'm adding two small cream/orange buck teeth peeking from under the upper lip, attached to the head bone, with the jaw hinge positioned near the front-aiming jaw joint. I'm also working out head proportions and vertical placement so it sits level with the back and shoulders, aligning head top height with the body's shoulder height so a bird could perch on top naturally.

Now I'm refining the head joint and neck chain coordinates to connect smoothly into the spine, adjusting chin and belly heights so the jaw and neck placement look proportionate against the body loft.

I'm working out the spine chain structure so it ends with a tip joint "spine3", with the neck chain parented to the last spine joint, then mapping out which bones form spans for the body loft versus which are just tip joints.

Now I'm checking that the body and head lofts overlap cleanly at the neck junction around z=0.48-0.50, making sure the body's rounded cap radius doesn't poke through the narrower head width.

Next I'm planning the cheeks as separate jowly fur spheres on each side of the head, true to capybara anatomy, and thinking through eye placement — small, high-set eyes per real capybaras, though the whimsical style might call for slightly bigger, more expressive eyes while keeping the cel-shaded toon paint consistent.

For the eyes, I decide against anime-style decals since they'd look oversized on a capybara, opting instead for my own storybook dot eyes: dark glossy spheres with small highlight dots and a subtle eyelid arc in coat color to give that sleepy, serene capybara expression.

Setting the lid to cover about the top 40% of the eye sphere, slightly larger radius than the eyeball for a natural overlap. Now I'm working out eye placement on the head surface — positioning them symmetrically along the sides near the top, checking that the coordinates line up with the head's loft width at that height so the eyes sit flush against the curved surface rather than floating off it.

Shaping the ears as flattened scaled spheres, tilted outward, with a slightly smaller inset of dark pink for the inner ear offset toward the outward side.

I'm settling on consistent world coordinates where x>0 is the left side, labeling joints accordingly like hipL. Then I'm adding a whimsical touch—a small chubby bluebird perched on the head, built from its own joint hierarchy (body, head, wings, tail, legs) parented to the main head joint.

I'm working out the bird's placement and proportions: positioning it near the top of the head between the ears, sizing the body and head spheres, and orienting it to face forward like the capybara.

Still shaping the bird's features...

Working out the tail geometry now — checking orthogonality of the extrude axes so the plate sits flat and angles upward slightly without distortion.

I'm also sketching tiny orange rod legs and toe nubs connecting the body to the head surface, then starting to define the joint hierarchy for the bird parts (body, head) so everything parents correctly.

Now I'm adding a jaw joint for the lower beak with upper and lower cone shapes, plus wing and tail joints parented to the bird body, assigning "wing" and "tail" roles while keeping the head role simple to avoid duplicating the capybara's head role.

For coloring, I'm planning a bluebird palette—cool blue back and wings with white edging, warm rust-orange breast, cream belly—to contrast with the capybara's warm brown fur, plus a small three-feather dark blue crest for charm. I'm also considering using cel() flat paint colors for parts, noting that paints don't count against the flat color limit so I have more flexibility there.

For the capybara's coat, I'm building a fur-edge paint that blends darker back brown into a lighter belly, with the normal-based fur direction giving it that storybook cel-shaded look, then layering subtle mottled variation on top for texture before considering grain for fur streak detail.

Then I'm planning fur tuft cards for cheeks, chest ruff, and rump, shaded by normal and tinted via a grey-to-color scheme — drawing simple flame-shaped SVGs in white with light grey strokes so they can be tinted by the coat's Paint color read at the root.

I'm deciding to use a non-cel, lit paint variant for the tuft tint rather than flat coat color, then scattering tuft hits across the body surface using a sweep-based scatter function with minimum distance and filter options, orienting each card's frame to face outward from the surface.

Working out tuft density: estimating body area at roughly 1.4 m², with a minimum distance around 0.07 giving up to 300 possible cards, but settling on ~220 cards with a bend count of 20 segments for a good balance of fuzzy silhouette detail versus performance, with root-tinted color paint applied per card.

For the coat palette, I'm picking warm reddish-browns for the back, lighter tan for the sides, cream for the belly, and darker brown for the muzzle and nose pad. I'm setting up a paint function for the head that darkens a stripe down the snout based on position and normal conditions, distinguishing forehead, cheeks, and muzzle tones.

I'm also adding a countershading gradient along the body's fur using the furEdge normal axis, keeping it subtle with a small period, and deciding to skip any ink outlining since brown-on-brown lines would look off. For the legs, I'm planning a darker brown gradient running down toward the feet.

Now I'm working out the head's structure as a series of loft stations in world space — starting with the skull and muzzle widths at different heights, placing the widest point at the cheeks, and continuing to define each station's position and dimensions to build out the head shape.

I realize the rounded cap at the path's end adds extra dome length equal to the endpoint radius, which pushes the nose tip too far out compared to capybara proportions. I need to rework the final station's width/height and reposition it so the added dome doesn't overextend the head length.

Switching to a flat end cap instead gives a blunt disk shape more fitting for a capybara's muzzle, with a separate flattened nose pad sphere layered on top to soften the edge. I'm redoing the station positions and dimensions with the flat-end cap...

Checking the total length though, I realize combining the body span with this new head length puts me around 1.55m, way beyond a real capybara's 1.0-1.3m range—I need to shrink the body so the rump sits closer in, targeting roughly 1.25m overall.

I'm reworking the hip position and loft stations, accounting for how the rounded start cap extends the rump backward by its radius, so I nudge the rump to z=-0.55 and adjust the width/height values at each station moving forward along the body.

I'm continuing through the remaining loft stations toward the neck, computing back-top and belly heights from center ± half-height, then laying out the spine chain (hips → spine1 → spine2 → spine3) and a neck chain branching from spine3 with their coordinates and bone names.

Checking the joint placement convention, I'm naming the neck joints and adding a head joint parented to neck2, noting the body loft only needs to extend up through the neck region since the head gets its own separate loft starting where the neck ends. Now I'm defining the head's station coordinates with widths and heights...

Working out the final length: with nose padding, total body length comes to about 1.4m, a bit longer than a typical capybara but acceptable for this whimsical chunky design. For height, I'm adding up the back, head top, and bird perch to get roughly 0.78m total, which feels reasonable compared to a real capybara's withers height once the bird and crest are factored in.

I'm positioning the bird on the head between the ears and eyes, centering its body around z=0.55 with its head slightly forward at 0.585. Then I'm calculating the eye placement using the head's cross-sectional radius at that z-depth to get the correct x-offset so the eyes sit naturally on the curved head surface.

Now I'm working out the nose pad geometry, sizing a darker ellipsoid slightly smaller than the head's tip so it protrudes just enough to read as a snout, then placing small nostril details on its front face.

Working out nostril placement and coloring, then placing a thin philtrum rod running down the center of the pad, calculating its surface positions at different heights.

Now figuring out the lower jaw geometry — using a tapered capsule sweep between the jaw joint and a forward point to shape the rounded lower lip area.

Setting jaw to center at y 0.355 with ry 0.035 gives a small protrusion below the head bottom, which feels right for a whimsical capybara look. I'm positioning the jaw bone joint and sweep path, then sketching a mouth line along the head's lip level using a curved sweep from nose side to cheek.

Checking the math, a lip line at y=0.37 sits closer to x≈0.076 than I expected since the head curves inward there, so a flat sweep path wouldn't follow the surface correctly. I'll switch to draping the mouth path directly onto the head's surface mesh so it naturally conforms to the rounded shape instead of guessing coordinates by hand.

I realize the hemisphere cap actually extends the tip length by the full radius while shrinking the cross-section, so I need to pull the path endpoint back to z=0.74, putting the chin tip around 0.815 — close enough to sit just under the pad.

Now I'm working out the two front incisors, positioning them as small boxes hanging from the lower lip pad down toward the chin, roughly at z=0.842 spanning y from 0.36 to 0.315.

Teeth sit just in front of the chin tip, which works fine visually, so I'll color them a slightly orange-cream tone. For the jowls, I'm adding small scaled spheres near the lower rear of the head using the same fur paint as the head itself rather than a separate tone, which should read as characterful cheek fluff without extra complexity. Next I want to add a small forehead bump (morrillo) as a subtle ellipsoid on top of the head.

Now I'm positioning the morrillo on the snout, calculating the surface height at that z-coordinate from the station profile and giving it a darker brownish tint. Then I'm working out ear placement by checking head width and top surface height at that station, sizing the ears as small ellipsoids positioned just outside the head profile.

For the ear tilt, I'm working out the rotation sign so each ear leans outward from the head center: using the right-hand rule, rotating the vertical ellipsoid about the z-axis by negative angle for the positive-x side produces outward lean, and mirroring the sign for the opposite ear.

I'm placing the inner pink ear piece slightly shifted toward the front-outer face so the opening reads as facing forward, checking it won't clash with the bird resting on the head since their coordinates stay separated. Then I'm adding cheek blush accents as small pinkish disks positioned below the eyes for a whimsical touch.

For whiskers, I'm sketching thin rod shapes extending outward and back from each side of the muzzle, using curved sweeps along a bone-nearest attachment so they follow the head's surface naturally.

I'm deciding to keep fur cards limited to the body and neck, skipping forehead and chin tufts for now, then moving on to feet details: designing a paw helper that builds a pad ellipsoid with small toe spheres and dark nail caps spaced along the front arc of each foot.

Now I'm positioning the nails as small forward-pointing cone spikes, and working out leg placement — shoulder joints need to sit inward from the body's half-width so the legs emerge naturally from beneath the torso rather than at its outer edge.

Checking the paw target distance against leg segment lengths, the reach is nearly maxed out with minimal elbow bend, so I'm bumping segment length to 0.14 each for a bit more slack and specifying the elbow bend direction as a backward-pointing vector, wrapped in a list to match the expected bends parameter format.

I'm working out the `limb` function signature—it takes root, target, lengths, bends, and an optional sole, returning an array of joint points. For chaining, I'm deciding to parent the front legs to the third spine joint (near the chest) and the hind legs to the hips joint, then building each leg as a polyline chain from the computed limb points.

For the hind legs specifically, I'm setting hip and target positions with lengths tapering from 0.15 to 0.09, noting the fold will bend the knee forward and the hock back, matching a capybara's fairly straight hind-leg posture. I'm also considering adding a haunch ellipsoid near the hind thigh to fill out the body silhouette where the loft tapers at the back.

Now I'm naming the joints and chains: front legs use shoulder/elbow/paw with L/R suffixes, hind legs use hip/knee/hock/foot, and I'm deciding to just call all four limbs "leg" chains, distinguishing them as "foreL" and "hindL". I'm also starting to think about adding a small tail nub via a sprout call.

For the tail, I'm planning a joint parented at the hips, positioned toward the back with a slight downward-backward direction, modeled as a small ellipsoid with the "tail" role. I'm also considering adding a perched bird made of scaled sphere parts, calculating where its feet and body should sit based on the head's top position so it looks properly perched.

Now I'm working out the bird's legs, feet, tail, head, eyes, and beak as small spike and sphere shapes positioned relative to the body, adjusting lengths and directions so the beak tapers forward naturally.

For the body coloring, I'm setting up a countershade paint with blue on the back and cream on the belly, then layering an orange breast patch based on surface normal direction to get that classic bird look.

For the head, blue cap transitions to a lighter face/cheek color higher up. Now I'm defining the wing shape as a teardrop outline for extrusion.

Still shaping wing polygon...

Working through wing placement math, I'm checking whether the plate sits flush against the body or protrudes outward, testing offsets around x=±0.046 to ±0.054 and considering an ellipsoid shape instead with tilt adjustments for orthogonality.

Adding stripe/tip color variation and planning a second smaller primary-feather layer offset outward on the wing.

For the tail, I'm working out three fanned feather plates with directions spreading backward and upward, computing orthogonal vectors so each feather extrudes correctly in a horizontal-ish orientation.

Each feather gets a narrow leaf-like hexagon outline with a cream tip band over a teal-navy base, attached at the rear of the body.

Now I'm adding a crest of three small spikes atop the bird's head, angled back, with a taller center spike and two shorter side ones in dark blue. Then I'm building the legs as thin orange rods dropping from the body with small forward-pointing toe spikes at the base.

I'm also tallying up the overall skeleton joint count across hips, spine, neck, head, jaw, legs, tail, and the bird parts, landing around 29, and considering adding ear and eyelid hinge joints for finer articulation.

Ears get their own bones parented to the head, with ear parts bound to them; whiskers stay jointless. I'm checking part counts stay manageable under budget, with toes and nails multiplying per foot but still fine, and making sure colors stay under the 64 flat-string limit by relying mostly on baked cel paints for shading rather than named colors.

Texel density checks out at roughly 2mm resolution across the painted body, which is plenty for small parts like toes. Now I'm defining an SVG fur tuft shape for the cards.

Still writing SVG code...

The stroke width scales to about 6px which works fine, and tinting with grey strokes gives a natural streaked look. I'm setting up the scatter parameters for the fur cards now — size range, lean, bend, variation, and a filter so fur only grows where the normal's y-component is above -0.4.

Scatter hits return Frame objects with `.at`/`.n` fields, and cards get built from those hits with the sweep target restricted to the head so points don't bury inside other meshes. I'm also planning whiskers as rod sweeps, plus eyes/lids tied to the head bone and ears jointed separately, with extra details like forehead tufts, toenails, and maybe a scarf still to add.

For a small whimsical touch, I'm thinking of adding a tiny flower tucked behind the left ear made of six flattened petal spheres arranged in a ring using trig-based positions, with a yellow center sphere.

I'll settle on placing the daisy near the right ear on top of the head, computing the surface height there, and arranging the petals as small elongated ellipsoids rotated radially around the flower's center to form a ring.

Now I'm working out eye highlights too — small white spheres positioned on the surface of each dark eye sphere, offset slightly outward and upward so they sit convincingly on the curved surface.

Adding one more tiny highlight. Thinking through eye orientation — keeping them dark all the way through since capybara eyes have no visible whites, with the pupil color set to a dark brown and the highlight angled toward front-outward for a forward-ish gaze. I'm also considering a subtle brow ridge above the lid using a small ellipsoid, then moving into defining the head's base fur coloring using the same edge-shading approach as the body.

Adding the coat blending and facial stripe logic...

Writing leg color blend logic...

I'm defining the shading function so lit areas use the base color while shadowed regions darken toward a fixed tone, then building out a color palette for the body—browns and tans for fur tones, a darker snout, dark nostril and eye colors, plus a separate palette starting for a bird character.

Writing palette constants and starting the main build function with careful imports to avoid unused-variable errors under strict TypeScript.

Defining joint hierarchy...

I'm switching to catmull-spline paths for the spine and neck chains to get smoother curves instead of rigid polylines, with the neck chain starting from the spine's tip joint and naming its segments neck1/neck2.

Now I'm adding joints for the head and jaw, positioning them along the forward-facing direction at the end of the neck, then adding hinge joints for the ears. I'm also starting to set up a body loft definition.

I'm checking that the loft's path through the hip, spine, and neck joints correctly aligns station widths and heights along the z-axis, confirming the path clamps properly when neck points extend slightly past the body's end.

The dome shrinking inside the head should stay hidden since the body's paint cel is smooth-shaded there, so it's effectively invisible. For the head loft I'm setting up a round start cap and flat end cap with the head bone and color, and considering bumping the circle sides from 8 to 10 for a less faceted look.

Now I'm sweeping the jaw geometry along a short path near the chin, tapering its radius slightly from front to back and tinting it a lighter cream paint color distinct from the head. The jaw sits just below where the head bottom ends, so I need to check that the two pieces connect cleanly.

Next I'm sketching small incisor bones near the head's mouth area and skipping lower teeth detail for now. Then I'm drawing mouth drape lines along the head's skull surface using a catmull-rom path with a thin ink-colored sweep, letting the bone weighting derive automatically from the head.

I'm now setting up a loop to mirror the eyes across both sides of the face...

Adjusting the lid to sit slightly lowered for a sleepy look, then adding blush and brow details before building ear joints with hinge roles and spherical ear parts scaled and rotated per side.

Working out the inner ear placement now, positioning a smaller pink ellipsoid on the outward-facing side of each ear so it sits just inside the outer ear shape.

I'm checking whether the ear base actually touches the head surface at that position, comparing the head's curved profile against the ear's bottom edge to see if there's an awkward gap I need to close.

Adjusting the ear to a lower center position so it embeds properly into the head, then setting the joint point accordingly. Now I'm shifting to whisker placement, figuring out base coordinates on the snout surface and the outward directions each whisker should point based on its side and vertical row.

Still defining whiskers... now sketching the rod helper with thin radius and pale cream color, using flat caps and a bone attachment so they follow the head. After that I'll skip eyebrow whiskers and move to the nose pad, deciding to paint it with a cel-shaded dark brown rather than a flat fill for visual consistency.

For material consistency, I'm settling on using cel-paint for most non-tiny parts while keeping flat color strings for small dark details, since both approaches get lit by the same scene lighting anyway. Now I'm scattering hit points across the body surface to place fur or detail cards, filtering them by some condition.

I'll settle on using bodyCoat here since the belly region mostly falls below n.y -0.2, so the filter naturally excludes it. I'm checking the scatter filter signature expects a function taking a hit with normal and position properties, which matches the docs example, and confirming scatter only excludes points inside the target mesh itself, not other nearby geometry like legs, so cards won't poke through unrelated parts.

Roughly 260 cards with a couple bend segments each gives about 2000 triangles total, which is fine performance-wise, and paint shading adds no extra cost. Now I'm sketching a helper function for generating paw toes, needing to import the Joint type from the skeleton module to type the joint parameter properly.

Writing paw toe geometry...

The direction literal checks out, but I need to drop the unused `s` parameter in the paw function to avoid a typecheck error. For the haunch spheres, I'm figuring out bone attachment to the hind thigh joint and checking that the scale and position give a rounded thigh bulge that protrudes slightly beyond the body silhouette without looking disconnected.

Now I'm setting up a similar shoulder bump geometry and verifying it doesn't poke too far past the body width at that z-station, then moving into defining the hind leg limb points and chain joints for the hip, knee, and hock.

Still writing sweep radii...

I'm checking that the chain's joint array type accepts a plain Vector3 array, and confirming the hip joint parent attaches correctly to the hips group even though the hip socket itself sits offset from the hips' local origin.

Building front leg limb calls...

Still positioning toes...

Now shifting to the tail — parenting it off the hips joint with a flattened ellipsoid shape for a simple nub. Then I'm moving on to the bird assembly, setting up the body joint parented to the head and starting to lay out head and jaw joints using similar positional offsets.

Writing wing and tail joints...

I'm confirming that explicit bone placement combined with world-position `at` values works correctly for nested geometry, then starting the bird's body shape — a scaled ellipsoid at the chest position painted with the bird coat material, covering belly and breast fluff too.

Now I'm sizing and positioning the head sphere, then placing the eyes and their highlights relative to the head center, checking that each eye protrudes slightly from the head surface and that highlight offsets stay within the eye radius.

Next I'm working out the bird's facial coloring: adding small pink cheek spots using position-based conditions, then defining a simple paint rule where the top of the head is blue, the face below is cream, with the cheek patches overriding those regions.

Now I'm placing the beak geometry — an upper cone and lower jaw piece positioned at the front of the head using spikes with specific lengths, radii, and bone colors — then adding small crest spikes angled back from the top of the head.

Next I'm working out the legs as thin rods from the belly down to the feet, with toe spikes extending forward and a back toe pointing backward, all colored in orange-tan, checking that they stay visible beneath the bird's belly ellipsoid.

Then I'm figuring out the wings: placing a wing plate extruded from the shoulder point backward along the body, sized and positioned to hug the narrower rear portion of the bird's body at the correct height and width.

Checking that the wing outline forms a valid simple convex polygon, then sketching the primaries outline similarly, placing it slightly outward from the wing joint with navy coloring, and confirming thickness direction doesn't matter since it's centered.

Now I'm defining how the wing surface gets painted — using the local x-coordinate along the wing to band it into cream, navy, and blue-dark stripes, then wiring that paint function through the shading/lighting resolver that applies lit versus shadowed color based on surface normal.

Moving to the tail, I'm setting up three symmetric feather extrudes anchored at a shared joint point, computing orthogonal direction vectors for each feather's orientation before extruding its geometry with thickness and bevel.

I'm typing the outline points array with an explicit type annotation and working out the daisy petal colors and head position geometry, calculating where the center sits on the curved top surface.

I need to check that the daisy doesn't overlap with the bird's ear or wing given their coordinates, so I'm nudging the daisy's x position slightly to clear the ear.

Actually, I'll place the daisy near the right ear at x +0.055, z .485, and define its eight petals as small flattened ellipsoids arranged radially around a yellow center sphere.

For the forehead I'm scattering tuft cards across the skull surface near the cheeks, filtering for areas with strong side-facing normals and positions below the eyeline, coloring them with headCoat (which includes a pink blush tint for cute cheek fuzz). I need to double check the default lean/bend direction for these cards so they flow naturally with the fur.

I'm confirming I'm skipping the chin tuft and texture import is correctly typed, then moving to wrap bodyCoat, headCoat, and legCoat with the cel shading function before checking the threshold logic for normal-based cel boundaries.

Now I'm writing the headCoat paint function, handling blush patches and a dark nose bridge region based on vertex position, making sure to rename unused normal parameters to avoid lint errors.

Writing headCoat paint logic...

Still defining the coat...

Defining more paint regions for the bird's head and tail, using position and surface parameters to split pink, blue, and cream patches across the coat.

I'm cataloging the flat colors needed for details like eyes, nostrils, whiskers, beak, and legs, counting around fifteen distinct hues. I'm also considering adding small fur tufts or a crown ridge near the top of the capybara's head, filtering by surface normal to keep them positioned correctly behind the bird.

Thinking it through, I decide to drop the crown tufts since they'd collide with the daisy placement, and skip lower jaw hairs for simplicity. For the nose pad, I'm adding a tiny gloss highlight to give it a wet, shiny look.

Placing more details...

I should skip whisker dots as unnecessary detail, and the toon ink outlines and bird shadow ideas don't apply here. The smile, blush, and half-closed eyes already cover the whimsical touches, and the hind foot and jaw positions check out fine, so I'm just confirming the sweep call's radius array is passed positionally and correctly formed.

Now I'm verifying the loft options support sides and caps properly, that bone references like head and hips resolve correctly with the type alias ordering, and that the `at:` coordinates and chain joint access all type-check cleanly before moving to the sphere geometry part call.

For the eyelid, I'm working out the geometry parameters (radius, segments, phi/theta ranges) and positioning it slightly forward of the eye center, then tilting it around the x-axis so the pole points toward +z, giving the lid a heavy, forward-leaning look that covers more of the upper front of the eye.

Now I'm moving to ear joint placements, confirming the card color option on the body, checking the body surface comes from the lofted sweep, and setting up deterministic scatter filtering using the head normal's x-component. For the teeth, I'm defining small box geometries with flat tooth coloring, positioned with a small gap between the two front teeth.

I'm double-checking vertical alignment so the teeth hang down without colliding with the jaw's chin cap, confirming the geometry stays clear near the mouth. I'll skip adding a dark mouth-slit detail for now, and I'm finalizing the function to return the root node. I also want to verify that the lowest points of the model -- foot pads, hind leg sweeps, and toes -- all touch or sit just above the ground plane.

I'm checking the reachability of both hind and front legs using distance calculations between hip/shoulder joints and foot targets, confirming the limbs fold within range. Then I'm starting to lay out the body loft stations with their widths and heights at increasing y and z values to build the torso shape.

Still refining loft stations and verifying the neck-to-head transition and skull proportions line up with the spine chain, then doing a final pass checking which helper functions (catmull, mix, mottle, paint, resolve, smoothstep) are actually used versus unneeded imports before writing the complete file.
